title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Depression Detection from Behavioral Signals: A Survey of Modalities, Datasets, and Evaluation Practices
content: Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) methods for detecting depression, classifying diagnostic status, and estimating symptom severity from behavioral signals have expanded rapidly, yet the resulting evidence base is difficult to compare because studies differ in input modality, dataset provenance, label definition, task formulation, evaluation design, and metric reporting. This survey systematically maps the field along these computational dimensions. Following a PRISMA 2020-aligned workflow, we searched Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (21 November 2025), screened 7,369 records, and included 195 studies that train and evaluate ML/DL models on audio/speech, text/language, and/or video/vision inputs, yielding 329 study-by-dataset entries and 1,039 extracted metric entries. We organize the literature with a six-dimensional taxonomy covering input modality, representation strategy, architecture family, fusion strategy, task and label formulation, and evaluation protocol, and we quantify the prevalence of each category under a strict explicit-only extraction protocol. The corpus is recent (71.3% of studies from 2022–2025), predominantly single-modality (72.0% of entries), and text-centered (41.6%); pretrained representations dominate (42.2%), and transformers, convolutional networks, and recurrent networks form the leading architecture tier. Binary depression-status classification outweighs continuous severity estimation, labels are grounded mainly in PHQ- and BDI-based instruments rather than formal diagnoses, and the DAIC/AVEC family accounts for 24.9% of dataset entries. After harmonizing class-specific and variant metric names, reporting concentrates on F1, accuracy, precision, and recall. However, 71.4% of entries lack explicit model–metric–context binding and 76.9% lack a clearly extractable primary metric. We conclude that the literature supports structural synthesis but not leaderboard-style claims of model superiority, and we distill open challenges and a minimum reporting checklist for future primary studies.
